assignment: Today the majority of humans own and operate cell phones on a daily basis. In essay form, explain if drivers should or should not be able to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.
essay_1:
Phones Belong in the Glovebox

Almost everyone I know carries a phone everywhere, and a lot of us feel nervous and unhappy when it is out of reach. That habit comes with us into the car. People think a quick look at a text or a short call is harmless, but it is a dangerous mistake. Driving is different. It is the one thing we do every day where a few seconds of distraction can kill someone. That is why I believe drivers should not use cell phones while driving, except for emergencies and a map that is set up before the trip starts.

The biggest problem is attention. When you drive, your brain has to keep track of speed, distance, other cars, people walking, signals, and the road all at once. Reading a text takes your eyes off the road for several seconds. On the highway, a car goes about the length of a football field in five seconds. A driver looking down that long is basically driving blind. A kid stepping off a curb or a car braking in front of you will not wait for you to finish typing.

Some people say hands-free calls fix this. Having both hands on the wheel is good, and it helps a little. The real issue is your mind, though. Studies show that people talking on the phone react slower and miss things right in front of them, even while looking ahead. Talking to a passenger is safer, because a passenger can see the road and usually goes quiet when traffic gets scary. The person on the phone has no clue what you are dealing with, and that is not safe.

Others say a rule like this would be hard to enforce, or that adults should be trusted to know their limits. That sounds fair, but trust does not protect a family hit by a careless driver. We already limit freedom on the road when one person's choices put other people in danger. Drunk driving laws and speed limits exist for the same reason. Most drivers who text think they are the exception, and that confidence is exactly what makes it dangerous.

There are fair exceptions. Calling 911 to report a crash or a fire should always be allowed. A map on a mounted phone, set before the car moves, is fine and no worse than a dashboard screen. Other than that, the phone should stay quiet and in the glovebox. When we put it away, we stay safe and protect the people we love. Getting home in one piece is the best reward, and it is worth more than any text.
essay_2:
Phones and Driving Don't Mix

Almost everybody has their phone on them all the time, and a lot of people freak out when they can't find it. We bring that habit into the car with us too. It seems like checking one text or answering a quick call isn't a big deal. But driving is something we do every day where just a few seconds of not paying attention could actually kill somebody. That is why I think drivers should not use their phones while driving, except for emergencies and GPS that you set up before you start.

The main problem is attention. When you're driving your brain has to keep track of a lot of things at once, like your speed, the cars around you, people walking, stoplights, and the road itself. Reading a text takes your eyes off the road for a few seconds. On the highway a car can go about the length of a football field in five seconds. Looking down that long is pretty much like driving with your eyes closed. A little kid running into the street or the car in front of you slamming on its brakes is not going to wait for you to finish your text.

Some people think hands-free calls solve the problem. It's true that having both hands on the wheel helps, but it doesn't fix the real issue, which is that your mind isn't on the road. Studies show that people who are really focused on a phone call react slower and miss things right in front of them, even when they are looking straight ahead. Talking to someone in the passenger seat is different because they can see the road too, and they'll usually stop talking if something scary happens. The person on the phone has no idea what's going on around you.

Other people say a law like this would be impossible to enforce, or that adults should get to make their own choices. But we already have rules for when one person's choices can hurt other people. That's the whole point of drunk driving laws and speed limits. Most people who text and drive think they're good at it and that nothing bad will happen to them, and that's exactly what makes it so dangerous.

There are a few exceptions that make sense. You should always be able to call 911 if you see a crash or a fire. Also, using a map on a phone that's mounted on the dashboard, as long as you set it up before you leave, isn't really worse than the screen that comes built into a lot of cars. Other than that, your phone should stay quiet and out of your hands. Nothing on your phone is worth someone's life, whether it's yours or a stranger's.
